messages.subject: PICs VS procD.pgls in Geomorph
parts:
Hi all,

I was comparing the result for beta coefficient (slope) of gls functions with the beta coefficient from regression computed on PICs (phylogenetic independent contrasts) and I was expecting them to be the same.
While other gls functions return beta coefficients equal to PICs beta coefficient, in the case of the function ProcD.pgls I believe I am doing something wrong as the beta coefficient differs.

The codes I have been using are the following:

lm(PICy~PICx-1)
gls(Y~X, dataframe, correlation=corBrownian (phy=Tree,method="ML"))
lm.rrpp(Y~X, data=data, Cov=vcvPhylo(Tree), SS.type = "I")

procD.pgls(Y~X, Tree, data=gdf)
procD.lm(Y~X, Cov= vcvPhylo(Tree) , data=gdf)

The first three functions return the same coefficients but procD.pgls and procD.lm do not. This confuses me as lm.rrpp should be the same function as procD.pgls or procD.lm (with a phylogentic variance-covariance matrix).

Any suggestions on what I might do wrong?
Many thanks in advance!

Bests,
Giada

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] PICs VS procD.pgls in Geomorph
parts:
Giada,

I believe you are looking at the OLS coefficients for procD.pgls or procD.lm.  These functions return both OLS and GLS coefficients but the geomorph functions do not have a S3 generic coef option.  In RRPP, nmle, and stats, the coef function works and in the case of RRPP, it knows to return GLS coefficients, if gls was used.   Interestingly, the coef function seems to work on procD.lm objects, even though coef.procD.lm was never designed, and it appears that it finds the OLS coefficients, thinking this is a class lm object.  Baffling!

Try this instead,

fit <- procD.pgls(Y~X, Tree, data=gdf)
fit$pgls.coefficients

but don’t use the coef function.  Because $coefficients exists, and because it is OLS, unlike $pgls.coefficients, the coef function searches for $coefficients and finds it, but returns the OLS coefficients.  Uncharacteristic of R, it does not verify the class of the object.

Thanks for bringing this to our attention!  I never realized this was possible!

Cheers!
Mike
